newsitem.title: USA: Clinton mulls more money for statistic agencies.
newsitem.headline: Clinton mulls more money for statistic agencies.

text.p: The Clinton administration is considering proposing stepped-up funding for government statistical agencies to study the consumer price index and other economic data, a senior official said Wednesday.
Franklin Raines, director of the White House's Office of Management and Budget, said the aim of the proposal would be to improve national economic statistics.

A congressionally appointed commission last week said that the CPI overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points annually, effectively costing the government billions of dollars in pension and other benefit payments.
Raines said that the administration was still studying the commission's report and indicated that it was unlikely to reach a conclusion soon.
"I don't see any benefit to try to rush it," he said.
He said that there were five or six different strategies for dealing with the CPI overstatement but that none of them has so far gained widespread support.
While experts agree that the CPI overstates inflation, they differ on the extent of that, with estimates ranging from 0.2 to 1.5 percentage points, Raines said.
"This is going to be hard work," Raines said, with the administration and Congress needing to work together on the issue.
"I'm not looking at this as a budget issue," he added. "We need to do this in a way that causes us to have broad support."
Raines argued that the atmosphere for tackling the Medicare problem has improved.
The Medicare trust fund, which helps finance health care spending for the elderly, is expected to go bankrupt in the year 2001.

Raines defended the administration's proposal to move some of the spending currently financed by the trust fund onto the general government budget. Republican lawmakers have attacked that proposal as a budget sleight of hand.
In a speech earlier to the Democratic Leadership Council, Raines painted an optimistic long-range outlook for the U.S. economy.
He argued that the United States was probably on the verge of achieving faster long-term economic growth as recent technological advances begin to bear fruit.
He also stressed the importance of a stable economic environment for the promotion of long-term growth, with prudent fiscal policy married to an appropriate monetary stance.
